passages.t: A snare at Mizpah: priests, people and king
passages.happening:
The LORD summons three groups: the priests, the house of Israel and the royal house. Judgment is against them, ‘because you have been a snare at Mizpah, a net spread out on Tabor’ (verse 1). The rebels are deep in slaughter, and God will discipline them all (verse 2).

He knows all about Ephraim. Israel has turned to prostitution and is defiled (verse 3). ‘Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God, for a spirit of prostitution is within them, and they do not know the LORD’ (verse 4). Their pride testifies against them, and Judah stumbles with them (verse 5). They go with flocks and herds to seek the LORD, ‘but they do not find Him; He has withdrawn Himself from them’ (verse 6). They have been unfaithful, and the New Moon festival itself will devour them (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 4 put the priests on trial. Chapter 5 widens the circle to the king's household and brings Judah into the charge beside Israel. The mood darkens from corrupt worship to what it brings: war, invasion and a useless search for help from Assyria.

Mizpah and Tabor were probably places of worship or royal government. Mount Tabor rises from the Jezreel Valley, and there were several places called Mizpah, which means watchtower. Snares and nets were the tools of a bird-catcher. The leaders who should have protected the people trapped them instead.

Verse 4 is one of the most searching lines in Hosea. Sin has become a habit that blocks the way back. The people still bring animals to sacrifice, but God has withdrawn. Religion without returning to him finds no one there. The New Moon was a monthly festival, and Hosea turns it into a picture of judgment, as if the feast will eat the people who keep it.
passages.later: The prophets warned that God would not be found by those who kept up the sacrifices and abandoned justice: ‘Bring your worthless offerings no more’ (Isaiah 1:13). Jeremiah later heard the same promise from the other side: ‘You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart’ (Jeremiah 29:13).
passages.asks: Verse 4 says their deeds would not let them return. Ask whether there is a habit in your life that has made it harder to turn back to God. And ask what it would mean to seek him and not only his help.

passages.t: The alarm sounds, and Assyria cannot heal
passages.happening:
The alarm sounds: ‘Blow the ram’s horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah’ (verse 8), and raise the battle cry in Beth-aven. Ephraim will be laid waste on the day of rebuke (verse 9). The princes of Judah are like men who move boundary stones, and God will pour out his fury on them like water (verse 10). Ephraim is crushed, because he is set on following worthless idols (verse 11).

‘So I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like decay to the house of Judah’ (verse 12). When Ephraim saw his sickness and Judah his wound, Ephraim turned to Assyria and sent to the great king. ‘But he cannot cure you or heal your wound’ (verse 13). God will be like a lion to Ephraim and to Judah. He will tear them and go away, and carry them off where no one can rescue them (verse 14). Then he will return to his place ‘until they admit their guilt and seek My face; in their affliction they will earnestly seek Me’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Verses 8 to 15 most likely reflect the Syro-Ephraimite war, about 734 to 732 BC. Pekah king of Israel and Rezin king of Damascus tried to force Judah into an alliance against Assyria and attacked Jerusalem. Ahaz of Judah appealed to Tiglath-pileser III, who crushed Damascus and took Galilee and Gilead from Israel. The scholar Albrecht Alt proposed that the alarm in Gibeah, Ramah and Beth-aven, towns of Benjamin on the road north from Jerusalem, describes Judah striking back into Israel's land, and that the boundary stones of verse 10 are Judah seizing land. Many scholars have followed him; others place the passage more broadly in the turmoil of those years.

Both kingdoms turned to Assyria. Menahem of Israel had paid heavy tribute to keep his throne, and Ahaz sent silver and gold from the temple to buy Assyrian help. Moving a boundary stone was a serious crime, because land was a family's inheritance from God. The great king matches a title Assyrian rulers used for themselves.

Hosea's pictures of God move from slow decay, a moth eating cloth and rot eating wood from inside, to a lion's sudden attack. That matches the history: long moral rot, then invasion. The last verse is quiet. God goes back to his place and waits for them to seek him.
passages.later: Second Kings tells of the war and the appeal to Assyria (2 Kings 16:5-9), and Isaiah met Ahaz in that same crisis (Isaiah 7:1-6). The law cursed anyone who moved a neighbor's boundary stone (Deuteronomy 27:17).
passages.hard:
How can God describe himself as rot, and as a lion tearing its prey?

The images are meant to disturb. Israel had come to think of the LORD as a safe presence at its shrines, one power among others that could be managed with sacrifices. Hosea shatters that picture. The God of the covenant is not tame, and when his people betray him, the covenant's own warnings come into force (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28). The prophets use the lion for God's judgment elsewhere too, and Israel would meet it in history through Assyria's armies.

Two things keep the picture from being the whole truth. God says he will tear and then go away to his place until they seek him; his purpose is their return, not their end. And the next verses, whether they are read as sincere or shallow, confess that the God who tears is also the God who heals (6:1). Readers differ on how to hold God's anger and his love together, but Hosea insists on both and will not let either cancel the other. These verses are about God's covenant with Israel. They give no one a way to read a particular person's illness or loss as God's attack.
passages.asks: Ephraim saw his sickness and went to Assyria for a cure. Ask where you go first when you see your own wound. And ask what it would take for you to seek God's face and not only relief.
